title: Phase Offsets Between the Minimum Light and Radial Velocity in Long Secondary Period Stars
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, submitted to ApJ
summary: Long secondary periods (LSPs), observed in a substantial fraction of luminous red giants, remain one of the longstanding problems in red giant variability. Previous studies have found a systematic phase relation between their photometric and radial velocity (RV) variations. We investigate this relation using ASAS-SN photometry and Gaia RV curves for 983 LSP stars, and compare it with other types of Long Period Variables. We confirm that LSP stars have a relatively narrow distribution of phase offsets between the phase of minimum RV and minimum light, with a mean value of $Δφ=-0.15\pm0.10$ in phase ($-0.96\pm0.64$ rad). Interestingly, this phase offset is similar for Miras, showing that this quantity is not sufficient to distinguish LSPs from pulsational variability. However, pulsating red giants show a relation between period and RV amplitude, with the RV amplitude generally increasing toward longer periods. LSP stars deviate from this relation, showing RV amplitudes of only a few km/s despite their long periods. The stacked light and RV curves of the LSP sample also show remarkable homogeneity and a coherent phase relation. In the binary interpretation of LSPs, the observed phase offset requires the obscuring material to be shifted in orbital phase with respect to the companion, consistent with models in which a low-mass companion produces a dusty wake in the wind of the red giant.

title: The Composition of M-dwarf Exoplanet Hosts: Atmospheric Parameters and O, Mg, Si, and Fe Abundances from IR Spectroscopy
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Determining M-dwarf abundances is an important step to discerning the chemical evolution of the Milky Way and characterizing exoplanetary systems, especially since these objects commonly host small exoplanets. However, a dearth of M-dwarf abundance measurements exist compared to Sun-like stars, partially due to their complicated optical spectra dominated by molecular absorption lines and low luminosities. To overcome these issues, we have obtained high resolution H-band spectra of 40 planet-hosting M-dwarf stars and 2 M-dwarfs in wide binaries with FGK primaries with IGRINS on Gemini South and on the McDonald Observatory 2.7m telescope, and NIRSPEC on Keck. Abundances were derived by comparing each observed spectrum to synthetic spectral grids generated with MOOG and MARCS atmospheric models. Effective temperatures were derived using OH and H$_{2}$O lines and [Fe/H] from Fe I and FeH lines. Both Mg and Si abundances were determined using atomic features. Overall, we find that our abundances are broadly consistent with previous literature M-dwarf abundances. We complemented our abundances analysis with UVW velocities and Milky Way stellar population membership probabilities and identified 2 potential thick disk stars from our kinematic and chemical analysis: GJ 1252 and L181-1 which was a previously known thick disk star. Kinematic stellar population probabilities and a low [Fe/H] abundance makes Kepler 42 a likely thick disk star, although uncertain Mg and Si abundances make classification difficult. Lastly, we have determined Si/Mg and Fe/Mg molar ratios for M-dwarf exoplanet hosts and find the abundance distributions leads to exoplanet core-mass fractions between 20 - 40$\%$.

title: MP-DualNet: A Dual-Branch Deep Learning Approach for Magnetopause Boundary Detection Using Simulated SXI Images
summary: The Earth's magnetopause is a key boundary governing solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer (SMILE) mission will provide global soft X-ray imaging of the magnetosphere through solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission, offering a new opportunity for remote sensing of magnetopause dynamics. However, the limited field of view (FOV) and variable observation geometry of the Soft X-ray Imager (SXI) pose challenges for reliable magnetopause detection. In this study, we develop MP-DualNet, an end-to-end dual-branch deep learning framework for automated magnetopause detection from simulated SXI observations. The framework jointly performs coarse localization to determine magnetopause visibility and relative position within the FOV, and fine-scale boundary localization through pixel-level segmentation. The model is trained and evaluated using line-of-sight magnetopause envelope maps derived from global hybrid simulations under different solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field conditions. The results demonstrate stable and consistent performance, with a classification accuracy exceeding 0.94 and a segmentation IoU above 0.97. For the test set, the mean absolute angular displacement from the reference boundary was 0.488 degrees. The model maintains robust performance across a wide range of noise levels and generalizes well, as demonstrated by its application to an independent storm event. These results indicate that MP-DualNet provides a reliable and generalizable approach for magnetopause detection in SXI observations, supporting future 3D reconstruction and space weather studies in the context of the SMILE mission.

authors: David L. Kaplan Patrick A. Woudt
title: Systematic Search for Cataclysmic Variables in Radio Surveys: First Radio Detection of IX Velorum
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 2 MRT tables (Tables 1 & A1), Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic search for radio emission from cataclysmic variables (CVs) across four wide-field radio surveys in the 0.7-4 GHz frequency range: VLASS; RACS; VAST; and EMU. We generated a reliable catalog of 2225 optically-identified CV candidates using a multi-stage cross-match, combined with systematic and manual verification; 1374 are matched to Gaia sources within the radio surveys' footprints. Among these, we detected six CVs in at least one epoch (at 1e16.5-1e17.5 erg/s/Hz, consistent with the typical population of radio-detected CVs); five had been detected in radio before. IX Vel, the closest nova-like CV, is detected in radio for the first time and shows quasi-persistent low-level emission across a 10 hr EMU (943.5 MHz) observation. Given most epochs detected no CV, we stacked images without radio detections to better constrain time-averaged brightnesses. We created co-added images and placed upper limits on low-level radio emission from each of the 423 individual CVs within the VAST footprint. To constrain the median brightness for the entire CV population, we combined all Gaia-matched CVs in each survey into single population-wide stacked images, detecting no statistically significant emission. Finally, we created population-wide image stacks of the CVs within 100 pc, using 14 epochs from 5 CVs in EMU to constrain their median persistent specific luminosity to <3e14 erg/s/Hz.

title: The JWST Early Release Science Program for Direct Observations of Exoplanetary Systems IX: A Multi-Wavelength Framework for Source Characterization in JWST Coronagraphic Imaging of the HIP 65426 System
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJL, 26 pages
summary: We present an updated analysis of the JWST coronagraphic imaging data of the HIP 65426 system. We aim to search for and characterize potential planetary companions as well as provide updated astrometry and photometry for the known exoplanet HIP 65426 b following updates to the JWST and spaceKLIP pipelines. Our measured photometry and astrometry show significant differences to those in Carter et al. (2023) but are consistent to within $2.2σ$ in separation, $1.5σ$ in position angle, and $3.7σ$ in flux. Our results indicate that pipeline updates have changed the photometry and astrometry significantly in some filters, especially in terms of observed flux. We see the greatest changes in separation in F444W and F1550C, position angle in F250M, and flux in F250M, F300M, F410M, F1140C, and F1550C. The SED of HIP 65426 b remains consistent with a young, giant planet best fit by models with a cloudy atmosphere and an effective temperature estimate of ~1436 K. Using both NIRCam and MIRI data, we identified 21 candidate companion sources in addition to the known planet. Of the 21 sources, 13 were attributed to astrophysical sources with eight background stars, four galaxies, one unknown, and zero planets. While one of these sources was detected in Chauvin et al. (2017), the remaining point sources were undetected in previous ground-based observations, which makes this work an initial epoch of astrometry for these objects. One galaxy in particular appears as a point source in MIRI but is highly extended in NIRCam and exposes a potential drawback to single-epoch MIRI imaging in a blind search for companions.

title: Unveiling the Origins of Local Group Galaxies with ELT-SHARP: An Overview of Science Cases
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. The ELT-SHARP project is led by the Milan Brera Observatory, and its white paper on the Local Universe has now been published in New Astronomy. It presents several science cases in a general way, including the MWLUDPSG initiative, with further tests and integration to follow in collaboration with the community
summary: The $Λ$CDM paradigm successfully describes large-scale cosmic structure, yet tensions possibly persist on galactic and sub-galactic scales. The Milky Way and the Local Universe offer a uniquely accessible laboratory to probe these discrepancies through chemo-dynamical studies of resolved stellar populations. Understanding disk assembly, dynamical heating, and galactoseismology requires wide-field coverage and high-angular-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy capable of penetrating dust-obscured regions and resolving crowded stellar environments. We propose science cases exploiting \textsc{SHARP}, a multi-mode near-infrared spectrograph for Extremely Large Telescopes and future space facilities. Operating over $0.95$--$2.45\,μ$m in a single exposure, \textsc{SHARP} enables efficient access to key stellar and gas tracers across the Galactic bulge, disk, halo, and nearby galaxies. The \textsc{NEXUS} mode provides adaptive-optics-assisted multi-object spectroscopy over a $1.2'\times1.2'$ field with spectral resolutions up to $R\sim17{,}000$, enabling gas and stellar kinematics. Complementarily, the \textsc{VESPER} multi-IFU mode delivers spatially resolved spectroscopy in crowded regions, allowing reconstruction of internal kinematics and stellar population gradients on sub-arcsecond scales. Combined with surveys such as \textit{Gaia}, APOGEE, LAMOST, LSST, 4MOST, and ELT--MOSAIC, this project will map six-dimensional phase-space structures of disk and bulge stars, stellar streams, and nearby disk galaxies (e.g. LMC, SMC). The data will enable investigations of bars, spiral arms, warps, flares, and satellite interactions, providing critical constraints on disk evolution, merger history, and dark matter substructure, and providing stringent tests of $Λ$CDM on the smallest accessible scales.

title: Black Hole Seeds and Little Red Dots: Connecting Formation and Growth with a JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Program
comment: Theory white paper on black hole seeds and Little Red Dots, submitted to the STScI call for JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury concept white papers as part of the Genesis Initiative (www.jwst-genesis.com). 5 pages (plus affiliations and references)
summary: JWST has revealed an abundant population of faint active galactic nuclei and a new class of compact, high-redshift sources known as Little Red Dots (LRDs), whose physical nature remains debated, with accreting massive black holes among the leading explanations. The emerging demographics of early black holes, with their high inferred number densities and, in some systems, the apparent excess of black hole mass relative to stellar mass, challenge simple scenarios of black hole seeding and growth. Despite these observational breakthroughs, the origin of early massive black holes remains uncertain, because "black holes have no memory": current samples cannot separate the imprint of seeding from subsequent growth. This white paper identifies the multi-cycle JWST observations needed to revolutionize our understanding of early black hole growth by: (i) distinguishing seeding pathways, (ii) constraining early black hole growth mechanisms, (iii) resolving the physical nature of broad-line emitters and LRDs, and (iv) testing black hole-galaxy co-evolution. These tasks require uniformly selected samples extending to low black hole and host-galaxy masses, allowing self-consistent measurements of black hole mass functions, Eddington-ratio distributions, and host properties. Grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and variability analysis through repeated observations of the same fields would provide complementary tests of black hole formation and growth, their connection to host-galaxy evolution, and the nature of newly discovered populations of LRDs. In this white paper, we argue that these joint tests require a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program; such a program could provide the depth, uniformity, and time baseline needed to place substantially stronger, complementary constraints on early black hole formation, growth, and their connection to galaxy evolution.

title: Thorium and Europium production in the early Galaxy: Implications for nucleocosmochronology
comment: 15 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary:
The ages of the oldest stellar populations can be investigated through nucleocosmochronology, with the thorium-to-europium abundance ratio providing a promising chronometer. We assess the reliability of log(Th/Eu) as an age indicator by testing whether thorium and europium were co-produced in a constant ratio in metal-poor stars, and evaluate the uncertainties affecting stellar ages.
  We present new Th and Eu abundance measurements for eight TITANS reference stars observed with UVES at the VLT. Combining these measurements with homogeneous literature samples, we investigate the behaviour of log(Th/Eu) as a function of metallicity. We derive ages adopting a theoretical initial r-process production ratio and assess the effects of observational uncertainties and sample statistics.
  At low metallicity, the observed Th/Eu ratios show no significant dependence on metallicity after excluding stars with anomalous actinide abundances, supporting broadly uniform Th and Eu co-production in the early Galaxy. The derived ages are consistent with expectations for an old, metal-poor halo population, although individual uncertainties remain substantial. Higher spectral resolution is needed to improve Th measurements, while combining stars in coeval populations can provide additional statistical gains.
  Nucleocosmochronology offers an independent approach to dating the oldest stellar populations. Homogeneous samples of coeval stars, particularly in globular clusters, observed with future high-resolution multi-object spectrographs could provide stronger constraints on the early formation history of the Milky Way and the age of the Universe.

title: An analytical framework for atmospheric tides on rocky planets. II. Semidiurnal thermotidal torque
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The thermodynamic acceleration induced by atmospheric thermal tides has a major impact on the rotation of temperate rocky planets, where gravitational and radiative tidal forcings are of comparable strength. This acceleration drives planets away from synchronous rotation, thereby affecting their climate, large-scale circulation, and surface conditions. These implications underline the need to better constrain the dependence of the thermotidal torque on the tidal frequency and on the physical parameters characterising the star-planet system, as this relationship remains insufficiently understood. In particular, the role of resonantly excited Lamb waves requires clarification due to its potential impact on Earth's length of day (LOD) during the Precambrian. Building on a previous work, which provided a fully analytical formulation of the atmospheric tidal response of rocky planets, we apply this framework to isentropic and isothermal atmospheres. We perform a comprehensive functional analysis of the resulting torque and compare the analytical predictions with numerical solutions from earlier general circulation model (GCM) studies. The analytical model agrees well with GCM results, accurately capturing the frequency dependence of tidal torque both for paleo-Earth and present-day Earth. More generally, the solutions capture the torque peak near synchronous rotation and the amplification associated with Lamb-wave resonance. Near resonance, the GCM results exhibit a stronger braking torque than accelerating torque. This asymmetry is reproduced by allowing tidal heating to lag behind insolation. The agreement with GCM spectra suggests that thermal tides in the benchmark simulations are driven predominantly by an indirect thermal forcing characterised by a substantial time delay, in contrast to the direct absorption of sunlight that dominates semidiurnal tides on present-day Earth.

title: SHARP(ening the) view of unresolved globular clusters in ultra diffuse galaxies
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Paper published on New Astronomy
summary: Ultra-Diffuse Galaxies (UDGs) challenge current galaxy formation models within the ΛCDM framework, particularly regarding their dark matter content and formation histories. Globular Clusters (GCs) serve as excellent tracers for probing the halos of these faint systems; however, current spectroscopic facilities struggle to reach the depth required to fully characterize GC populations beyond the local neighborhood. In this work, we present the scientific potential of NEXUS@SHARP, a near-infrared multi-slit spectrograph proposed on the upcoming Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). We demonstrate that NEXUS is uniquely positioned to overcome current observational limitations by combining high spatial resolution with efficient multiplexing. We show that NEXUS can efficiently help to characterize the GC population in UDGs across diverse environments out to 60 to 70 Mpc - with a few hours of ELT time. These capabilities will allow for precise measurements of radial velocities and stellar populations, enabling robust dynamical mass estimates and distinguishing between competing UDG formation scenario.

title: The obscured nucleus of NGC3256 S. I. Anisotropic AGN near-IR radiation field traced by CO v=1-0 with JWST/NIRSpec
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 9 pages, 5 figures
summary: The southern nucleus of NGC3256, a nearby luminous infrared (IR) interacting system (d=40 Mpc; L(IR)=10^11.6 Lsun), hosts a deeply obscured low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) associated with a massive and fast bipolar collimated molecular outflow. JWST/NIRSpec observations revealed bright spatially resolved ro-vibrational CO v=1-0 4.67um emission at the base of this molecular outflow extending out to ~300pc, which is excited by the ~4.7um IR radiation from the southern dusty core. Using Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) models, we analyzed the CO v=1-0 band emission to determine the intensity of the ~4.7um IR radiation field across the outflow base. We find that the core spectral luminosity density at ~4.7um, as seen by the material in the outflow base, is ~2-4 times higher than that inferred along our line of sight, indicating an anisotropic near-IR radiation field. Moreover, the slower than d^-2 decrease of the near-IR flux density across the outflow base suggests a collimated radiation field, for which we estimate a small half-opening angle (15-20deg) and a diameter of the collimating structure of 15 +- 5 pc. This is slightly smaller than the diameter of the obscuring envelope (25 +- 5 pc). Combined with the expansion of this obscuring envelope, traced by the blueshifted CO v=1-0 absorption toward the nucleus, this suggests that the AGN is beginning to clear its environment. We estimate N_H~10^22-23 cm^-2 for NGC 3256 S, which is similar to that of Type 2 AGN. However, in contrast to Type 2 AGN, a high covering factor of the obscuring material, possibly sustained by inflows linked to the galaxy merger, and similar to that expected in deeply obscured compact obscured nuclei (CONs), is needed to explain the absence of extended high-ionization emission. Therefore, NGC 3256 S shares properties with CONs and Type 2 AGN.

title: Cepheid Metallicity in the Leavitt Law (C-MetaLL) survey: X First spectroscopic characterization of Galactic Type II Cepheids and calibration of the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity relations
comment: Article proposed for acceptance in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 12 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables
summary:
Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are Population II pulsating stars that serve as distance indicators through their period--luminosity relation. Along with RR Lyrae stars and the tip of the red giant branch, they offer an independent route to the Hubble constant, helping assess systematic uncertainties in its determination.
  We aim to investigate the impact of chemical composition on T2Cs' period--luminosity relations by building a homogeneous spectroscopic sample of Galactic T2Cs with iron and oxygen abundances.
  We observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with UVES at the ESO Very Large Telescope. For 74 stars, we derived stellar parameters and iron and oxygen abundances through a self-consistent spectroscopic analysis based on equivalent widths of absorption lines. This sample nearly doubles the number of T2Cs with spectroscopic metallicity measurements available in the literature.
  We used these abundances to test theoretical predictions for the instability strip and, together with $Gaia$ parallaxes, to derive Period--Wesenheit--metallicity (PWZ) relations. In agreement with theoretical predictions, the metallicity coefficient ($γ$) is small and statistically consistent with zero in all relations, ranging from approximately $-0.02$ to $+0.17$ mag dex$^{-1}$. We also estimated distances to 22 Galactic Globular Clusters hosting T2Cs, finding agreement within uncertainties with independent literature estimates.
  Our results show that metallicity has, at most, a minor impact on T2Cs' pulsation properties and distance scale, supporting their reliability as Population II distance indicators.

title: Coordinated Space and Ground Monitoring of Accretion Bursts in a Protoplanetary Disk: MIRI and iSHELL observe the long-term modulation of gas within a small inner disk cavity
comment: Accepted for publication on ApJ
summary: DQ Tau is a TTauri eccentric binary with pulsed accretion bursts regulated by its $\sim 16$-day orbital period. We have monitored this system with seven instruments from ground and space over 40 days. We present results on molecular gas variability from nine JWST-MIRI and nine IRTF-iSHELL epochs over three sequential accretion bursts with accretion luminosity pulses increasing by factors of $\sim 9$-80. A fundamental new measurement from this analysis is the line broadening of CO (from iSHELL) and H$_2$O (from MIRI) lines, which we use to estimate Keplerian radii and their variability in parallel to the line luminosity. This unprecedented dataset clearly shows that the molecular emission does not react like HI and the 5-$μ$m continuum with each accretion burst: the line luminosity and width of all hot molecular gas tracers decrease over $\sim30$-35 days, consistent with an emitting region decreasing in temperature and mass as it recedes to larger radii within the $\sim 0.2$-0.4 au inner cavity perturbed by the binary. The infrared molecular spectrum of DQ Tau is affected more by disk dynamics then by chemical changes triggered by variable accretion, supporting model expectations for chemical relaxation timescales that are much longer than the duration of these accretion bursts ($\gg 10$ days). The variability observed in all tracers in this study is consistent with a scenario where gas mass builds up near the disk edge to modulate the burst peak intensity and gas density in the inner cavity every $\sim4$-5 orbital periods. The origin of this modulation is still unclear.

authors: Nuno Miguel Andrez de Oliveira Covas
title: Why a Multi-Cycle Treasury Program is Essential to Maximize JWST's Scientific Contributions to Galaxy Formation
comment: The Genesis Initiative (https://www.jwst-genesis.com) is an extragalactic community-wide effort to coordinate white papers in response to the STScI MCT concept call. This framing white paper, with two companion Genesis theory white papers, sets the stage for MCT programs and has been submitted to STScI
summary: The Genesis Initiative is an extragalactic community-wide effort to coordinate white papers in response to the STScI Multi-Cycle Treasury (MCT) concept call. Two of JWST's primary science goals are to discover and characterize the first stars and galaxies, and to understand how they evolved into the galaxies we see today - questions whose fundamental importance has been affirmed by the past three decadal surveys. JWST's first five years have surpassed expectations, revealing a bounty of unexpected discoveries about the early universe. Yet these discoveries have raised as many questions as they have answered, and key mission goals remain unmet. Transforming this excitement into a quantitative physical understanding of early galaxy formation requires a uniform, statistically controlled legacy dataset that the current portfolio of smaller, heterogeneous programs cannot provide. The history of the Hubble Space Telescope offers a clear precedent. Its most transformative extragalactic results came from large, coordinated surveys far exceeding what the standard time-allocation process typically approves, and these uniform datasets remain scientifically productive decades later. We argue that JWST is now poised for the same leap. Answering the field's central open questions demands coordinated, community-led surveys of ~1000-2000 hr, with uniform and well-characterized selection functions that are structurally impossible within single-cycle programs. Such an investment is time-critical while JWST's instruments remain at peak performance, and would maximize synergy with ALMA, Euclid, Roman, Rubin, and future facilities. We therefore urge STScI to open a MCT channel, enabling the bold, ambitious surveys needed to understand how galaxies evolve from first light to the present day.

title: AGN Archaeology: A Systematic Search for Fading AGN in MaNGA
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures (+2 appendix figures), 2 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) vary on broad timescales, but are primarily thought to "flicker" on and off during episodes of high and low accretion. Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) which are actively accreting material often show optical spectra dominated by AGN emission in their nuclei and beyond. In this work we develop an empirical model to quantify the fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra using the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) emission line diagnostic diagram. We leverage this model against integral field unit (IFU) data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey to select 34 galaxies with weak nuclear AGN activity relative to their AGN signatures at large radii; this signifies past AGN activity which is fading with time (i.e., fading-AGN). The majority of our fading-AGN reside in edge-on systems undergoing minor mergers. We construct a simple model consisting of a disk galaxy with ionization cones and find that the orientation of such a system will impact its BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU observations. The mean distance to the extended AGN emission in our sample corresponds to a light-travel time of $1.1\times10^4$ years. We use this to set a lower-limit on the typical lifetime of the AGN phase ($t_{\text{AGN}}>1.3\times10^5$ years) which is consistent with SMBHs growing via brief accretion bursts. These fading-AGN allow us to probe the elusive period of post-AGN galaxy evolution, and they give a $\sim10^4$ year baseline for understanding the accretion history in these systems.

title: Survey of Surveys Data Release 3. Homogenised stellar parameters across nine spectroscopic surveys
comment: Submitted to A&A. 20 pages, 17 figures, 5 tables
summary: Large spectroscopic surveys have measured atmospheric parameters for millions of Milky Way stars, but differences in instruments, wavelength ranges, analysis methods, and assumptions introduce survey-dependent systematics that complicate their joint use. We aim to place effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity estimates from major spectroscopic surveys onto a common, externally validated scale, and to provide a homogenised catalogue for large-scale Galactic studies. We construct the calibration hierarchically. We first define an internal reference scale from the best-populated and best-overlapped surveys (APOGEE, GALAH, and LAMOST LRS), and model survey-to-reference corrections and their uncertainties with machine-learning regression. The scale is then extended to LAMOST MRS, Gaia RVS, RAVE, DESI, Gaia-ESO, and SEGUE, and anchored to high-quality measurements from the PASTEL database. The calibration reduces survey-to-survey offsets and improves consistency in independent overlap samples: independent calibration of GALAH and LAMOST LRS temperatures onto the APOGEE scale reduces their median offset from 44.5 K to 6.2 K. The final catalogue contains about 10.13 million stars, including 6.10 million in the recommended high-quality subset and 3.69 million in the metallicity-optimised subset. For the high-quality subset, Gaia benchmark stars give median residuals of 30 K in $T_{\rm eff}$, 0.03 dex in $\log g$, and $-0.02$ dex in [Fe/H]. The [Fe/H]-optimised subset gives median residuals of 0.003 dex against Gaia benchmark stars, 0.05 dex for globular clusters, and $-0.02$ dex for open clusters. As an example application, we confirm the presence of metal-poor stars on thin-disc-like orbits, including stars with [Fe/H] $< -2$, showing that the catalogue can be used to study rare Galactic populations on a consistent multi-survey scale.

title: Using Structure Functions to Characterize Protoplanetary Disk Velocity Residuals
comment: Accepted to ApJ
summary: Protoplanetary disks, the birthplace of planetary systems, are highly dynamic environments. High angular and spectral resolution observations have revealed non-Keplerian motions in nearly every source studied, indicative of (magneto-)hydrodynamical instabilities or planet-disk interactions. However, these velocity perturbations rarely exhibit ordered structure, limiting our ability to attribute them to a specific mechanism. We propose the second-order structure function as a tool for recovering structural properties of velocity perturbations in the presence of significant noise. Using morphological models, we demonstrate how easy-to-calculate heuristics and parametric model fits together identify structure in noisy data and recover its properties, including correlation lengths, their radial scaling where genuinely present, and the anisotropy. We further outline a workflow to de-noise the data and to build a matched null model against which inferences are compared. Applying the framework to one numerical simulation each of the gravitational, magneto-rotational and vertical-shear instabilities, we recover their structure at high significance and the structural heuristics separate all three pairs, with the gravitational and vertical-shear instability simulations remaining the hardest to distinguish once observationally degraded. As a demonstration on real data, 12CO observations of TW Hya reveal azimuthally elongated velocity structure that persists once the large-scale m=1 component is removed. We also delineate where a Gaussian description breaks down for coherent features such as spiral arms, and how inclination affects the recovered heuristics. The methodology is implemented in the eddy package and provides a foundation for statistically characterizing turbulent velocity structure in high-resolution disk observations.

title: On the importance of medium-resolution continuum spectroscopy for JWST's extragalactic legacy
comment: White paper submitted to the "Multi-Cycle Treasury Program Concepts with JWST" call, Nov 2026
summary: We argue for a significant investment of JWST time into an extremely deep medium-resolution NIRSpec MSA survey targeting a large, representative sample of high-redshift $(z>1.5)$ galaxies, specifically intended to obtain high-SNR continuum detections. This is only possible with JWST, and no planned future instrumentation has similar capabilities, meaning that obtaining such observations with JWST must be urgently prioritised. The vast majority of existing archival NIRSpec observations are not deep enough for continuum science, being focused on the detection of emission lines. Deeper continuum data opens up the ability to constrain a much wider range of key galaxy physical parameters, including stellar population ages and metallicities, stellar kinematics and neutral gas physical properties, inflows and outflows. Such measurements will provide crucial insight into quenching physics, galaxy dynamical masses, merger histories, pristine early star-formation, reionization and the physics of Little Red Dots, as well as enabling all of the emission-line science that can be achieved with shallower observations. To facilitate future survey planning, we present an empirically derived relationship between rest-optical continuum SNR in JWST NIRSpec medium-resolution data, rest-optical apparent magnitude and exposure time, which we show to be independent of redshift (and hence the grating used). We then provide a 1000-hour sketch survey plan based on achieving the continuum SNR $=20$/pixel necessary to constrain key physical properties and scaling relations for a large galaxy sample at $z>1.5$. We finally discuss NIRSpec sky subtraction strategies, which are of critical importance for continuum SNR.

title: A multi-epoch VLBI study of compact symmetric objects as contaminants in the search for milli-lenses
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, submitted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The Lambda Cold Dark Matter model predicts a high abundance of low-mass dark matter halos, which can be probed through milliarcsecond-scale gravitational lensing (milli-lensing) of background radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The Search for MIlli-LEnses (SMILE) project aims to find these rare systems with Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). However, compact symmetric objects (CSOs) can closely resemble milli-lenses in VLBI images and are the main contaminant in such searches. We aim to determine the nature of the nine remaining milli-lens candidates of the SMILE pilot study and to characterize their physical properties. We analyzed all available multi-epoch, multi-frequency archival VLBI data, new HSA and EVN observations, and single-dish and connected-element interferometer measurements. We tested the lensing hypothesis through the morphology and spectra of the sources, and characterized their kinematics, spatially resolved spectral indices, magnetic fields, and integrated spectra, using synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) and free-free absorption (FFA) models. We identify eight of the nine candidates as CSOs, four of them for the first time. Spectral index asymmetries between components and previously undetected emission connecting them rule out the lensing hypothesis. Only J0923-3435 remains ambiguous. For the CSOs with known redshifts, the lobes have equipartition magnetic fields of $\sim$20-320 mG and projected separations of $\sim$60-240 pc, and show no measurable expansion, implying kinematic ages of at least $\sim$50-950 yr. The integrated spectra of J0210-2213 and J2347-1856 favor an inhomogeneous external free-free absorber over homogeneous and inhomogeneous SSA models. Since CSOs will be the main contaminant in the full SMILE survey, applying this framework will provide the same constraints for a much larger sample of compact radio-loud AGNs.

title: Mass loss in AF supergiants: At the verge of the Eddington limit and still with weak line-driven winds
comment: 13 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We study global atmosphere models of AF supergiants. In agreement with previous studies, we found super-Eddington layers in the photospheres of these stars, which lead to density inversions. Our tests showed that the super-Eddington layers are caused by hydrogen ionization. The analysis of radial perturbations has not revealed any instability of such layers, but we show that super-Eddington layers in an optically thick environment are prone to instabilities due to nonradial perturbations. We predict the wind parameters of AF supergiants from our global wind code with a comoving-frame radiative force. Despite the existence of density inversions, the predicted mass-loss rates are significantly lower than those estimated from observations. Theoretical values approach the observational estimates only for the most luminous supergiants, which are close to the Eddington limit due to light scattering on free electrons. Part of the discrepancy between the mass-loss rates could be attributed to the influence of the clumping on the observational properties. Low mass-loss rates imply that the winds of AF supergiants may be strongly influenced by the magnetic fields, suggesting an explanation for the observed spectral variability of these stars.

title: No Significant Rotation of the Spiral Structure in the IM Lup Protoplanetary Disk
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Spiral structures are often observed in protoplanetary disks, but their origins remain uncertain. Yoshida et al. (2025) reported a pattern speed consistent with local Keplerian rotation for the $m=2$ spiral in the dusty disk around IM Lup using multi-epoch ALMA observations, supporting a gravitational instability (GI)-driven origin. However, recent studies revise the disk geometry of IM Lup, motivating a reassessment of its spiral pattern speed. In this study, we reanalyze the disk geometry of the same multi-epoch data using visibility-based continuum emission modeling. The inferred disk geometries differ from those adopted in previous studies by a few degrees but are consistent across epochs and with recent independent estimates based on gas emission analyses. The revised geometries yield weaker residuals and more physically plausible radial spiral phase profiles. Unlike previous studies, our remeasured spiral pattern speeds are consistent with zero rotation within the uncertainties. We conclude that the previously reported Keplerian-like motion can be explained by a mismatch in the adopted disk geometry, which affects the spiral phases measured in Band 6 (2017, 2019) and Band 7 (2024) differently. In addition, we identify a tentative large-scale one-armed spiral-like structure extending beyond the known $m=2$ spiral, which may provide clues to additional perturbations, such as an embedded planet or late-stage infall. Future high-resolution Band~6 observations with a longer time baseline will be essential for more accurately determining the spiral pattern speed.

title: Detection of Differential Chromatic Refraction with LSST Camera data
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The Earth's atmosphere acts like a prism, deflecting blue light towards the zenith more than red light. Airmass-dependent changes in astrometry can therefore be used to infer additional information about the wavelength distribution of light within a photometric passband. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will observe each point in the southern sky several hundred times, with observations spread across a range of airmasses. Using commissioning data from the LSST camera released in LSST Data Preview 2, we report the detection of this differential chromatic refraction (DCR) effect in observations of galaxies and quasars in the COSMOS field. We show how information from DCR can complement the six-band colour information from LSST and help break degeneracies when selecting extragalactic samples and estimating their photometric redshifts. DCR will be a valuable resource for scientific studies and care should be taken not to remove useful DCR information from future LSST data releases.

title: DOWSING, Dust Observations With SCUBA-2 In Nearby Galaxies: I. Dust in M81
comment: 18 pages, 21 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS on 2 November 2026
summary: We present a resolved far-infrared/sub-millimetre study of dust in the nearby spiral galaxy M81 using Herschel PACS/SPIRE and JCMT SCUBA-2 observations from 70 to $850\,μ\mathrm{m}$. We model the dust emission using both single-temperature modified blackbody (SMBB) fits and point process mapping (PPMAP), comparing pixel-by-pixel SED-fitting with image cubes of dust surface density as a function of position and temperature. For fixed $β= 1.9$ and a dust opacity of $κ_{350\,μ\mathrm{m}} = 1.92\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}$, SMBB gives an integrated dust mass of $(1.77 \pm 0.09) \times 10^{7}\,M_\odot$, while PPMAP gives $(2.65 \pm 0.13) \times10^{7}\,M_\odot$. The higher PPMAP mass is expected because real lines of sight contain dust over a range of temperatures, whereas SMBB assumes a single effective temperature and can underestimate the dust mass. Both methods show enhanced dust surface densities along the spiral arms and a radially declining dust temperature, with the warmest dust in the central region. Variable-$β$ fits indicate only moderate spatial variation in $β$ for well-constrained pixels, but the strong $T$-$β$ degeneracy motivates a fixed emissivity index for the main analysis. Combining the dust maps with HI data, we find a positive radial gas-to-dust ratio gradient, with $d\log_{10}(\mathrm{GDR})/dR = 0.065\,\mathrm{dex}\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-1}$. Comparison with M81's metallicity gradient implies a declining dust-to-metals ratio, potentially consistent with more efficient grain growth in the inner disc. The star formation rate is modest, $\sim 0.27\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, and is strongly concentrated along the spiral arms. These results suggest that the dust, gas, and star-forming structures of M81 are strongly shaped by its spiral arms, while the central region hosts the warmest dust in the disc.

title: Photometric eclipse-center variations over the long cycles of Magellanic double-periodic variables
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Double-periodic variables (DPVs) are interacting binaries with an orbital modulation and a longer cycle of uncertain origin. I searched for long-cycle-dependent eclipse-center variations in Magellanic DPVs and tested whether changing disk brightness can produce analogous shifts with fixed conjunctions. I analyzed Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) photometry for 109 eclipsing-DPV candidates. In separate long-phase intervals, I measured centers of eclipses by profile fitting to local flux minima ($Q$) and by shifting a fixed eclipse template ($T$). A single synthetic semidetached DPV provided a separate numerical experiment. Of 49 curated systems with sufficient timing data, 27 show at least one $Q$ or $T$ modulation under the adopted procedure. Some selections depend on the fitting choice, but ten systems retain a selected $Q$ curve with all tested local functions and windows. Three have both estimators selected in both eclipses, without establishing whether conjunction times change. Using local color interpolation, 14 of 16 systems measured in both eclipses are redder at the deeper, phase-0 eclipse. In the artificial system, fixed conjunctions coexist with large photometric shifts and quadrature-brightness changes, although the large tilted-disk cases do not reproduce the selected observed crossing phases. Long-cycle-dependent photometric eclipse-center variations occur in a substantial fraction of the evaluable, curated sample, not necessarily of all DPVs. Circumstellar brightness changes can produce such shifts, but the single artificial system neither fits an observed DPV nor establishes disk tilt as the cause. Genuine conjunction-time changes remain possible in individual objects.

title: Prospects for detecting hot-Jupiter tidal decay through transit timing with the mission Earth 2.0
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures
summary: Orbital decay of hot Jupiters provides a unique opportunity to probe tidal dissipation in star-planet systems. However, despite extensive observational efforts, only one hot Jupiter, namely WASP-12b, currently exhibits conclusive observational evidence for orbital decay. Expanding this sample is therefore crucial for establishing a statistical understanding of tidal interactions in planetary systems. Long-term transit timing variations (TTVs) provide a direct observational probe of orbital decay induced by tidal dissipation between a hot Jupiter and its host star. The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission will revisit the original Kepler field, delivering high-precision transit timing measurements and extending the observational baseline to approximately 24 years (2009--2033). In this work, we aim to assess the capability of ET to detect orbital decay in hot Jupiters previously observed by Kepler. We generate four years of simulated ET light curves based on the expected photometric precision and observing cadence of the mission and analyze them jointly with archival Kepler and TESS observations. Using these combined datasets, we perform long-term TTV analyses and predict the achievable precision for measuring orbital period variations. We find that ET can substantially improve the precision of orbital decay measurements in hot Jupiter systems by a factor of 7.2. Assuming the stellar tidal quality factor inferred from previous observations, ET is expected to detect orbital decay in three additional hot Jupiter systems. The expanded sample of hot Jupiters with measured orbital decay will establish ET as a powerful probe of tidal dissipation in star-planet systems, providing tighter constraints on stellar tidal quality factors and new insights into the tidal evolution of hot Jupiters.

title: MapHub: Daily Relevance Heatmaps of New arXiv Preprints for a Research Community
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure, submitted to RNAAS
summary: MapHub, the MIDAS arXiv Preprint Hub, assesses each day's new arXiv submissions for every participant in a research community, with a large language model reading each paper against portfolios built for the participants. It publishes the relevance scores, from 0 to 100, as a heatmap that shows whose work each paper touches. In the authors' blind ratings, the top 10\% of papers by MapHub's scores held about 70\% of the raters' own top 5\%, pooled, against about a third for a text-matching baseline. About 6\% of a day's astro-ph papers reach 30 for each participant, and one every three days reaches 60. MapHub runs on a standard Claude subscription and is designed to be useful for any field: https://github.com/kailicao/maphub-public.

title: The HST-Hyperion Survey: X-ray AGN Enhancement in the Hyperion Proto-supercluster
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to ApJL
summary: Dense environments can influence both galaxy evolution and supermassive black hole growth, but whether they enhance or suppress (or both) active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity at high redshift ($z\gtrsim2$) remains uncertain. We identify X-ray AGN using the deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy Survey and combine optical/near-infrared (NIR) photometry and photometric redshift information from COSMOS2020 with extensive ground-based spectroscopy and HST-grism observations. Redshift information is incorporated statistically using a Monte Carlo framework. We find a higher X-ray AGN fraction in Hyperion ($7.4^{+3.2}_{-1.8}\%$) than in the coeval field ($3.2^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\%$), corresponding to a $\sim2.3σ$ difference. Strikingly, this enhancement is concentrated in the overdense peaks, where the X-ray AGN fraction reaches $12.3^{+5.5}_{-3.4}\%$ ($15.0^{+6.9}_{-4.4}\%$ in the most massive peaks versus $6.2^{+11.9}_{-2.1}\%$ in the less massive peaks), while the lower-density Hyperion outskirts ($2.1^{+3.6}_{-1.1}\%$) show no evidence of enhancement relative to the field. These results add to the limited but growing evidence for enhanced AGN activity in high-redshift protostructures, suggesting that the dense environments at these epochs may preferentially trigger AGN during the early stages of cluster assembly.

title: Source Imaging of the Multiple Type-II Solar Radio Bursts and their Multiple CME-Shock Signatures in the Corona
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: This study reports the meter-wavelength radio imaging of multiple type-II bursts occurred on 01 October 2011 observed by LEARMONTH radio spectrograph in the frequency range of 180 - 25 MHz, with two coronal shocks from two coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the nearby active regions lying adjacent to each other. The two CMEs are well observed by STEREO and LASCO FOV. The eruption is associated with the multi-peaked soft X-ray flare erupted from N16W45 (first and second C3 and C6 class flares) and from N09W04 (third one an M Class flare). The first type-II burst starts during the impulsive phase of the first flare and the second type-II burst starts during the peak time of the third flare. The drift rate of the second type-II burst is larger than that of the first type-II burst. The EUV images at AIA 211 reveal the shock-like EUV wave structure along the north-western limb around 09:06 UT, the first type-II appearing around the same time (09:06 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave and as an outward propagating wave along the disk around 09:55 UT, the second type-II appearing around the same time (09:55 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave. According to the simultaneous EUV and radio imaging data the radio sources appears along the nose-front of the shock like EUV wave structure for the first type-II burst and for the second type-II burst they are located along the shock flank. The second event is strongly affected by the projection and scattering effects, the corrections are achieved by applying spherical cone model and 3D Monte Carlo ray-tracing code for turbulent solar environment at fundamental frequency.

title: Results from a Stellar Occultation by (623) Chimaera
summary: We present results from a stellar occultation by the asteroid (623) Chimaera on October 21st, 2025, when it passed in front of V magnitude 13.86 star UCAC4 626-004193. Chimaera is the largest asteroid in the Chimaerid asteroid family and will be subject to a spacecraft flyby in the 2030s. Eighteen telescopes were deployed, spanning the United States from Arizona to North Carolina, incrementally spaced by $\sim4.4$\,km with respect to the cross-track of the shadow. In total, sixteen telescopes collected useful data. This multi-chord observation, when compiled into a single sky-plane plot, suggests a profile which is well-described by an elongated elliptical fit, with a semi-major axis $a=26.2\pm0.8$ km and a semi-minor axis $b=16.0\pm1.0$ km. The projected area from ellipse fitting is 1316 km$^2$, and a limb fit is calculated to enclose 1312 km$^2$. Photometry collected in the Gaia G band over a seven-month period coinciding with the occultation corresponds to a geometric albedo $p_G=0.059\pm0.005$; comparing with archival occultation observations and direct observations gives $p_G=0.051\pm0.004$ and $p_V=0.051\pm0.004$. We compare occultation sky-plane projections with 3-D modeling from inversion techniques and demonstrate that the models can accurately predict the orientation of Chimaera at the time of each occultation.

title: Preliminary Goniopolarimetric Simulations for Space Weather Radio (SWARA) Polarimeter
comment: 10 pages, 10 figures, URSI-RCRS 2026, IIG, Mumbai, India, 17 -20 November, 2026, Selected but not presented
summary: Goniopolarimetry is a technique that measures the direction-of-arrival (DoA) using the polarization properties of the incident electromagnetic (EM) waves. This study aims to incorporate the technique of Goniopolarimetry for our proposed polarimeter, Space Weather Radio (SWARA) Polarimeter, to provide early warnings for space weather or solar events. We have performed preliminary simulations for a tri-monopole antenna configuration. The behaviour of the tri-monopole antenna with varying signal-to-noise (SNR) ratios along the field-of-view (FOV) was investigated using simulations. The angular localization error (ALE) variations, along with SNRs, were simulated to quantify the sensitivity of the Goniopolarimetric algorithm to galactic background noise. Future work will focus on determining the optimum effective length of the individual monopoles to maximize sensitivity and localization accuracy while ensuring efficient impedance matching with the receiver. The optimized antenna will be evaluated under realistic plasma environments through electromagnetic and plasma simulations to investigate the influence of plasma parameters.

title: The ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST Survey: The Tully-Fisher Relation at $z = 4-6$
comment: 13 pages, 6 Figures, 2 Tables, Accepted for Publication in A&A
summary: The Tully-Fisher relation provides a fundamental link between galaxy mass and their kinematics. Although its evolution is relatively well constrained up to cosmic noon, observational probes at higher redshifts remain scarce. In this work, we investigate the stellar and baryonic Tully-Fisher relations (TFRs) at $z=4-6$ by analyzing JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of 18 main-sequence star-forming galaxies belonging to the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST survey. We apply a morpho-kinematic disk classification scheme, finding five disk-like galaxies and a survey disk fraction of $0.28\pm0.11$. These disk galaxies span stellar masses of $10^{9.5-10.5}\,M_\odot$, intrinsic rotational velocities of $91-127\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, and intrinsic velocity dispersions of $66-129\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. For both versions of the TFR, we find that the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST disks lie below the local relations and are likely offset from those reported at cosmic noon ($z\approx2.3$). By fixing the TFR slope to the $z=0$ value, we measure zero-point offsets for the stellar-mass TFR of $-0.96\pm0.18$ dex and $-0.50\pm0.18$ dex relative to the local Universe and cosmic noon, respectively. For the baryonic TFR, we find zero-point offsets of $-0.57\pm0.20$ dex and $-0.30\pm0.20$ dex with respect to the local Universe and cosmic noon relations. Our measurements are consistent with the redshift evolution of the zero-points of both TFRs being driven by the evolution of dark matter halo properties with cosmic time, modulated by a reduced contribution of dark matter to the dynamical mass on the galaxy scale.

title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited
comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Previous studies combined rotation periods derived from Kepler photometry, stellar parameters from previous Gaia Data Releases, and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive to conclude that statistically planet-hosting stars rotate slower than stars without detected planets. Here, we revisit these studies by using similar Kepler rotational period sample, but with an updated Gaia DR3-based stellar parameter catalogue and an updated exoplanet catalogue. We apply minimal sample cuts in evolutionary state, metallicity, and distance, and then model the stellar rotation period as a function of effective temperature alone. For each star, we derive the ratio of its observed period to the temperature-expected period, and compare the ratio distributions for the planet-host and non-host stars. For periods shorter than 20 d, the planet-host distribution of this ratio is shifted towards longer periods; the period-ratio median is ~15% larger for hosts than for non-hosts (p_KS = 2.4 x 10^-4). We also examine the recently published TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS) and find a similar trend. However, the strongly structured period distribution precludes a robust comparison between the host and the non-host stars. Therefore, the updated analysis, using more robust stellar and planetary parameters, recovers the previously reported association, strengthening the case for a genuine connection between stellar rotation and planet occurrence.

title: Evolution of Dust In Protoplanetary Disks With Magnetized Winds
comment: 23 pages, 13 Figures. Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: Observations and theory increasingly indicate that protoplanetary disks are weakly turbulent, implying that magnetized disk winds may dominate their angular momentum transport and long-term evolution. Yet dust evolution in wind-dominated disks remains poorly understood, despite its importance for planet formation. In particular, whether wind-dominated disk evolution can create regions with enhanced dust-to-gas mass ratios that enable planetesimal formation via the streaming instability is unclear. We build a parametric hybrid disk evolution model that includes turbulent accretion, wind-driven accretion, and wind-driven mass loss to investigate dust evolution in magnetized protoplanetary disks. We employ this model to carry out a parameter study in which the initial total accretion rate, the wind-driven mass loss rate, and the turbulence strength are varied. We find that although wind-dominated disks are more favorable to dust growth and concentration than turbulence-dominated disks, conditions suitable for the streaming instability arise only within the inner few au and only under the most extreme conditions: very weak turbulence ($α_\text{turb} = 10^{-5}$) where magnetized winds drive most of the accretion ($\dot{M}_\text{acc,tot} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{wind,acc}$), and wind-driven mass loss comparable to the accretion rate ($\dot{M}_\text{wind,outflow} \simeq \dot{M}_\text{acc,wind}$). Our results therefore imply that, beyond the inner few au, the parametric wind-driven evolution models considered in the literature do not by themselves produce conditions suitable for planetesimal formation via the streaming instability, motivating more physically complete models in which spontaneous, long-lived dust traps can arise.

title: GALI Localization of Off-Grid GRB Directions: A Comparison of Rectangular and Triangular Calibration Meshes
comment: SPIE Proceedings 2026
summary: Rapid localization of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) is essential for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger follow-up, but combining wide sky coverage with accurate localization remains challenging. GALI (GAmma-ray burst Localizing Instrument) determines source directions from count-rate modulations caused by internal shadowing in a three-dimensional scintillator array. We investigate a triangular calibration mesh based on an icosphere tessellation of the hemisphere and compare it with the rectangular mesh used previously. The triangular mesh samples the hemisphere more isotropically and gives better interpolation between calibration points. Laboratory measurements with the full-scale GALI detector yield an average angular separation of $0.86^\circ \pm 0.14^\circ$ for random source directions, compared with $1.19^\circ \pm 0.28^\circ$ for the rectangular mesh. Monte Carlo simulations of 50,000 randomly distributed GRBs in realistic low-Earth-orbit background conditions, each with 1000 detected counts, give average angular separations of $1.91^\circ \pm 1.20^\circ$ and $2.73^\circ \pm 2.18^\circ$ for triangular and rectangular meshes, respectively. The better laboratory performance is partly attributed to its approximately 3-4 times higher detected counts. Additional simulations indicate sensitivity from 10 keV to $\sim$1 MeV, with a peak effective area of about 130 cm$^2$ near 100-150 keV. A compact 1U GALI implementation also achieves degree-scale localization in simulations, demonstrating the concept's potential for CubeSat-based GRB and multi-messenger missions.

title: Feedback-Driven Star Formation and YSO Distribution around H II Regions Sh2-140 and Sh2-145
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, Accepted for publication in Bulletin de la Société Royale des Sciences de Liège
summary: OB2 associations are ideal sites for studying various star-formation processes. Here, we study the region containing the bright-rimmed cloud (BRC) 44 and the dark cloud LDN 1204, which lies between two H II regions, Sh2-140 and Sh2-145. The region is a part of a larger Cepheus OB2 association. Our previous study on BRC 44 suggests a scenario of triggered star formation through radiative feedback. Using the infrared data from the Spitzer Space Telescope and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer, we find a spatial correlation between the locations of massive stars and the distribution of young stellar objects, indicating a possible sequential pattern of star formation across the region. These results indicate the role of massive-star feedback in shaping the star-formation history of the complex

title: The cold substellar frontier in JWST Extragalactic surveys: a robust parallax measurement yields the most distant known ultra-cold Y dwarf
comment: 36 pages (including 9 pages of appendices), 18 figures, 11 tables, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We present an analysis of JADES-GS-BD-5, an extremely cold Y dwarf identified in the JADES/GOODS-South field. Using multi-epoch JWST/NIRCam imaging spanning a $\simeq2$-yr baseline, we calibrate the JWST astrometry and obtain the first robust parallax measurement for a brown dwarf discovered in a JWST extragalactic deep field. We measure a proper motion of $μ_{\rm tot}=49.8^{+0.3}_{-0.3}$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and a parallax of $\varpi=15.7^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ mas, corresponding to a geometric distance of $d=64^{+6}_{-5}$ pc, $\sim3\times$ further than that of the previously known most distant Y dwarfs with parallax-measured distances. We hence determine a tangential velocity of $v_{\rm tan}=15.0^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ km s$^{-1}$, consistent with a Galactic thin-disk object. We find no evidence for binary acceleration, significant photometric variability, or a plausible host. The $J$-band spectral morphology of JADES-GS-BD-5 is consistent with existing Y-dwarf templates, while its extremely faint luminosity and overall near-infrared spectral profile confirm that it is one of the coldest dwarfs discovered to date. We therefore adopt a classification of $>$Y1, consistent with a NIRCam colour-based proxy of cY1.5. The robust parallax-determined distance allows us to determine its bolometric luminosity, $\log(L_{\rm bol}/L_{\odot})=-7.08^{+0.09}_{-0.09}$. Evolutionary modelling places JADES-GS-BD-5 in the planetary-mass regime and makes it a rare benchmark for the study of cold giant-planet atmospheres. Current atmospheric models fail to reproduce its SED in detail, pointing to the importance of disequilibrium chemistry and vertical mixing. Finally, we also report additional proper motion measurements for eight of the other nine known JADES Y-dwarf candidates, highlighting JWST extragalactic surveys as a powerful route to building a statistically useful, parallax-calibrated sample of Y dwarfs.

title: BeAR: The Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code - A GPU-accelerated framework for low-resolution, high-resolution, and joint retrievals of exoplanet atmospheres
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: We present BeAR, the Bern Atmospheric Retrieval code and successor of Helios-r, and its new high-resolution cross-correlation framework for emission and transmission spectra. BeAR performs joint retrievals by adding the log-likelihoods of high- and low-resolution data computed from the same model atmosphere. The framework implements established cross-correlation log-likelihoods, with the line-depth scaling either fitted analytically or sampled as a free parameter, their per-pixel generalization, fast model filtering, and model re-injection adapted to this filtering. The forward model and likelihood run entirely on a graphics processing unit (GPU). One forward model takes about 1 ms on an NVIDIA GH200, allowing millions of models per minute on a GPU cluster. In separate retrievals of Gemini South/IGRINS and JWST/NIRSpec dayside spectra of the hot Jupiter WASP-77Ab, BeAR reproduces published abundances, C/O ratios, and metallicities to within 1.5 sigma, the preference for 13CO, and the thermal structure and line contrast to within 1 sigma. The joint retrieval confirms a sub-solar metallicity and a near-solar C/O ratio. A full IGRINS retrieval with 17 free parameters takes 27 to 42 minutes on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080 or about 14 minutes on eight RTX 4090 GPUs. Injection--recovery tests show that the posteriors underestimate the uncertainties of abundance ratios by about a factor of two.

title: Design and Commissioning of the BURSTT-256 Main Antenna Array for the Fast Radio Burst Survey in the Local Universe
comment: 22 pages, 14 figures; submitted to PASP
summary: The Bustling Universe Radio Survey Telescope in Taiwan (BURSTT) is a radio interferometer array designed for surveying fast radio bursts (FRBs) in the nearby Universe with a wide instantaneous field of view (FoV) of $\approx$6000 deg$^2$ and precisely localizing them with sub-arcsecond angular resolution. The first phase of BURSTT, BURSTT-256, consists of a main antenna array comprising 256 log-periodic dipole antennas (LPDAs) observing at 400-800 MHz for real-time beamforming and FRB search, currently with 256 beams covering $\approx$ 3200 deg$^2$ FoV, together with several smaller outrigger stations with 16-64 antennas and separated by $\mathcal{O}(10^2 - 10^3)$ km baselines for joint observations to localize FRBs using very-long baseline interferometry. This work presents the design, deployment, and commissioning of the BURSTT-256 main array, including site selection, radio-frequency (RF) background characterization, receiver antenna array and RF front-end, as well as real-time, factorized digital beamforming backend that currently generates 256 beams. The system's on-sky performance, sensitivity, and beamforming fidelity have been calibrated through observations of bright celestial calibrators. The antenna array in the initial phase using commercial LPDAs has a system equivalent flux density of $\approx$11 kJy, and is expected to achieve $\approx$4 kJy using custom-design LPDAs after optimization in late 2026. BURSTT-256 serves as a critical pathfinder for future expansion of the array to 2048 elements and beyond, operating at 300-700 MHz with $\approx$6000 deg$^2$ FoV. It establishes the framework required to discover and localize nearby FRBs with sub-arcsecond precision. By substantially increasing the number of well-localized nearby FRBs, BURSTT will facilitate multi-wavelength and multi-messenger counterpart identification, helping to unveil the elusive origin of FRBs.

title: Formamide formation on forsterite and Mg(OH)$_2\cdot$H$_2$O
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. Formamide formation in the Universe has been the subject of debate due to its importance as a precursor to amino acids and RNA. Current studies focus on the gas-phase and icy grain formation routes. However, formamide formation on bare silicate surfaces or hydrated Mg-bearing molecular models remains largely unexplored in environments relevant to protoplanetary disks. Aims. This study presents a quantum-chemical investigation of formamide formation on an Mg center and a silicate surface. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the bare (010) forsterite ($Mg_2SiO_4$) surface, used as an analog of a bare dust-grain surface, may promote formamide formation via $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. Methods. I employed density functional theory (DFT) to study the addition of $NH_2$ to $H_2CO$ with an isolated $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ molecular model and on the forsterite (010) surface. First, I benchmarked various theoretical methodologies. I then examined the ability of $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the forsterite (010) surface to promote formamide formation. Finally, for the case with an entrance barrier, I computed unimolecular rate constants and half-lives to assess its kinetic behavior. Results. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ promotes proton transfer within the $NH_2$-$CH_2O$ intermediate via the O-H group coordinated with Mg following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$, whereas on the forsterite, a barrier-less addition pathway is found when $NH_2$ is initially physisorbed close to the formaldehyde center, followed by proton transfer leading to formamide formation. Conclusions. The Mg-bearing model systems considered here can promote rapid proton transfer following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. For the $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ model, the reaction step from the pre-reactive complex is predicted to occur on nanosecond timescales at temperatures approaching 300 K. The present work provides kinetic data for astrochemical models.

title: The Composition of M-dwarf Exoplanet Hosts: Atmospheric Parameters and O, Mg, Si, and Fe Abundances from IR Spectroscopy
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Determining M-dwarf abundances is an important step to discerning the chemical evolution of the Milky Way and characterizing exoplanetary systems, especially since these objects commonly host small exoplanets. However, a dearth of M-dwarf abundance measurements exist compared to Sun-like stars, partially due to their complicated optical spectra dominated by molecular absorption lines and low luminosities. To overcome these issues, we have obtained high resolution H-band spectra of 40 planet-hosting M-dwarf stars and 2 M-dwarfs in wide binaries with FGK primaries with IGRINS on Gemini South and on the McDonald Observatory 2.7m telescope, and NIRSPEC on Keck. title: Inertial sub-range detection and characterization for ground-layer turbulence at new extremely large telescope sites in Chile
summary: The atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) presents turbulence regimes that diverge from the classical Kolmogorov 1941 (K41) power-law spectrum widely assumed in optical atmospheric profiling, yet turbulence characterization for astronomical applications remains predominantly based on K41 assumptions. Using high-frequency sonic anemometer data from site-testing campaigns at the Giant Magellan Telescope (GMT) and Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) sites in Chile, we apply detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA)---a technique from fractal time-series analysis---to identify the inertial sub-range and evaluate statistical isotropy in the ABL, comparing our approach with the Fourier-based algorithm for robust identification of the inertial subrange (ARIIS). Strict Kolmogorov conditions---simultaneous isotropy and $k^{-5/3}$ scaling across all fields---are satisfied in fewer than 7 per cent of observations. DFA-detected regime transitions correlate with characteristic turbulence scales, providing objective, model-free boundaries for the inertial subrange. Comparative $C_n^2$ estimation reveals that structure function methods assuming K41 scaling diverge significantly from flux-based parameterizations under stable conditions. title: CosmicGrain: An On-the-fly Dust Physics Module
summary: We present CosmicGrain, a dust physics module built on Gadget-4 that models explicit dust superparticles that experience resolved gas-dust drag and radiation pressure, undergo collisional heating and cooling with gas, and are further shaped by subgrid treatments for grain growth, thermal sputtering, coagulation, shattering, supernova shock destruction, and astration. We run an eleven-rung physics ladder (S0-S10) at 1024^3 resolution to isolate the contribution of individual processes to a Milky Way-mass halo's dust population. Because dust is evolved as active on-the-fly particles, individual grains retain distinct histories producing results inaccessible to passive dust models such as the strongly asymmetric silicate-to-carbon shattering destruction ratio driven by silicate grains' smaller birth size. Gas-dust drag is the dominant driver of ISM dust enrichment, increasing dust levels by ~100 times while every other process changes the R200 dust abundance by only 10-30%. We find reasonable agreement with the Milky Way's radial dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios, with carbon dust preferentially enriching the CGM relative to silicates. The code is freely available at https://cosmicgrain.space.

title: First Results from JACKS: A VLA Ammonia View of Gas Heating and Star-forming Cores in the Central Molecular Zone
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures. Included in International Astronomical Union Proceedings Series: Traversing the Galactic Center in Space and Time, Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 405
summary: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) combines warm molecular gas, strong turbulence, and a star-formation rate below that expected from its dense-gas reservoir. Its K-band setup covers the metastable NH$_3$ $(1,1)$--$(5,5)$ inversion transitions, five non-metastable NH$_3$ lines, the 22-GHz H$_2$O maser transition, H64$α$ and H66$α$, and broad continuum windows. The nominal resolutions are approximately $1.5''$ ($0.06$ pc at the Galactic Centre) and $0.4$ km s$^{-1}$ for the NH$_3$ lines. We present preliminary imaging products that demonstrate water-maser self-calibration, compact and extended continuum emission, filamentary NH$_3$ structure, and complex compact sources with multiple velocity components. title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited
comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Previous studies combined rotation periods derived from Kepler photometry, stellar parameters from previous Gaia Data Releases, and planet hosts from the NASA Exoplanet Archive to conclude that statistically planet-hosting stars rotate slower than stars without detected planets. We apply minimal sample cuts in evolutionary state, metallicity, and distance, and then model the stellar rotation period as a function of effective temperature alone. For periods shorter than 20 d, the planet-host distribution of this ratio is shifted towards longer periods; the period-ratio median is ~15% larger for hosts than for non-hosts (p_KS = 2.4 x 10^-4). We also examine the recently published TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey (TARS) and find a similar trend. However, the strongly structured period distribution precludes a robust comparison between the host and the non-host stars. Therefore, the updated analysis, using more robust stellar and planetary parameters, recovers the previously reported association, strengthening the case for a genuine connection between stellar rotation and planet occurrence.

title: The infrared unmodulated pyramid wavefront sensor: simulations, lab and on sky
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 16 pages, 21 figures, 7 tables
summary: Direct imaging of Earth-like exoplanets requires strong suppression of stellar light at small angular separations, achievable with extreme adaptive optics (XAO). title: GetGaia 2.0: automatic membership and systemic motions of stellar systems with Gaia
comment: 22 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to A&A. The code will be available at https://github.com/AndresdPM/GetGaia2

title: The Pristine survey XXXI. A stream offset from the Stream: very metal-poor stellar debris trailing 100$^{\circ}$ from the LMC-SMC system
comment: Submitted to A&A. 12 pages + 7 pages appendix (10 Figures, 3 Tables). Comments are very welcome! Note: Abstract is shortened to comply with the arXiv character limit
summary: Context: The stellar counterpart to the $200^\circ$-long HI Stream from the Clouds probes their tidally stripped stellar populations and constrains their interaction history and structure before infall into the Milky Way. Aims: We investigate the chemodynamics and possible origin of very metal-poor (VMP; [Fe/H] $<-2$) stars in the stellar Stream, targeting distant red giants selected from the Pristine--Gaia synthetic metallicity catalogue. Methods: We obtained high-resolution Gemini/GHOST spectroscopy of 33 candidate members, deriving radial velocities and metallicities. We combine these data with literature red giant members and assess their association with the Clouds using orbital integrations in a time-dependent Milky Way--LMC potential. We also compare their distribution with collisionless test particles initially placed in a diffuse LMC stellar halo. Results: We identify 12 high-confidence members based on energy and angular momentum: one intermediate metal-poor star ([Fe/H] $\sim-1.6$), ten VMP stars, and one extremely metal-poor (EMP) star ([Fe/H] $<-3$). The new VMP stars trace over $100^\circ$ of the trailing Stream, follow the Clouds' kinematics, and lie $\sim20^\circ$ from both the HI Stream and previously known, more metal-rich debris, suggesting a metallicity-dependent spatial distribution. Combined with the literature, they approximately double the known red giant sample and extend its metallicity range from [Fe/H] $\sim-0.5$ to $-4.3$. Orbital integrations support an association with the Clouds, while test particles reproduce the debris' broad spatial distribution. Conclusions: VMP and EMP stars contribute to the Clouds' tidal debris. They may originate in the extended stellar halos of the LMC or SMC, or in disrupted satellites. Their spatial and kinematic properties can constrain future simulations of the Milky Way--LMC--SMC interaction.

title: Mitigating scanning-induced systematics in Hipparcos and implications for Gaia astrometry
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Space-based astrometric missions such as Hipparcos and Gaia rely on one-dimensional scanning strategies that couple the measured signals with both observation times and scanning geometry. This coupling can introduce spurious periodicities and complicate their interpretation. We present a non-parametric extension of the phase-distance correlation (PDC) periodogram that quantifies and reduces dependence on scan geometry at the period-search stage. Using Hipparcos data, we identified recurrent periodicities associated with characteristic scanning-law timescales and showed that they are strongly suppressed by the scan-angle-controlled statistic. We then applied the method to Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) prerelease epoch astrometry, where a recurrent ~54-day feature is suppressed across multiple sources while independently known orbital signals remain detectable. The method provides a diagnostic of scan-angle dependence and a way to mitigate its impact on period searches. These results are particularly relevant for Gaia DR4, where public epoch astrometry will enable large-scale searches for companions ranging from exoplanets to dormant black holes.
